name: Wei Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and fit timber canopies and covered walkways on building sites. My vocational trade certificate got me started; the overhead shifts pay more than ordinary carpentry, though I'm a fitter rather than a team lead. I like making a dry path for people; checking slings in a gust slows everyone down for good reason.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a medical practice and our children are grown. We have about nine months of expenses saved and many similar local building jobs. I use AI every day for board counts and lift sketches, then check the supports myself; I hope to stop regular site work around 67 if our retirement income and my health allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can count canopy boards and save a morning, and I already use it for that. A quick count is useful, but I still choose the fixing that holds overhead timber safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My overhead site shifts pay above the usual carpenter rate, my partner works at a medical practice, and we have nine months of expenses saved. Our children are grown and there are plenty of builders nearby, so I can keep aiming to leave regular sites around 67 if the income adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the covered walkway at the transport interchange and use my daily AI list to check board counts against the measured supports. My partner and I will add a new amount from each full paid month to our home repair reserve while both incomes hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this year's work and curious whether the list gets a bit better. I'm still responsible for every overhead fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a board list miss a support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI list counted the standard beams but missed a brace beside the bus platform. I changed the order before the lift began.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would a new reserve deposit come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra deposit would be from next month's wages after our ordinary bills, not money shifted out of the nine-month reserve. If overhead shifts fall, we pause the new deposit.

say: **AI board counts** can save time while overhead timber still needs safe fixings.
The worker remains responsible for the **actual brace** and lift.
think: My **higher site pay** and partner's medical-practice income support our bills.
Nine months of **saved expenses** and nearby builders give retirement planning room.
do: **Fit** interchange canopy and check daily AI list against measured supports.
**Deposit** new money from full paid months while both household incomes hold.
feel: **Calm** about current income and modest daily AI gains.
S0.quote: The AI list counted the standard beams but missed a brace beside the bus platform.
fieldNote: He checks a **daily AI list** against overhead supports before the lift, catching a missing brace.
His **new deposits** come from future full wages if both incomes hold, separate from nine months already saved.

steps.text: Fit interchange canopy and check daily AI list against measured supports
Deposit new money from full paid months while both incomes hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI will order more timber and schedule lifts before robots can fix overhead canopies. A builder should let the carpenter correct a plan when the beam is different from the drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid fitting role looks secure, and nearby builders need people who can work at height. The new office planner may hurry a lift, which worries me for safety more than for our household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll learn the contractor's updated AI lift-planning controls on an unused bay and compare the crane reach with our tape measurements. If the proposed sequence ignores a brace, I'll correct the plan before the crew works beneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a rushed lift, but calm about wages. I like testing a tool early so the first live canopy isn't the experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the lift plan misses a brace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the lift, check the sling and move the marker on the plan before the crane operator tries again. A green schedule cannot hold a timber canopy up when the sling is loose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why test the new controls on an unused bay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The unused bay has no pedestrians below it, and the crane reach is easy to measure there. I'd record each edit before using the program on the transport entrance.

say: **AI scheduling** changes before robots fix canopies overhead.
Carpenters need **edit authority** and a safe stop for lifts.
think: My **paid fitting role** still looks secure with plenty of local builders.
A rushed **crane sequence** threatens safety more than my immediate income.
do: **Learn** updated AI lift controls on unused site bay.
**Compare** proposed crane reach with tape measurements before overhead work.
feel: **Uneasy** about lift safety while household income stays secure.
S1.quote: A green schedule cannot hold a timber canopy up when the sling is loose.
fieldNote: He takes **new AI learning** into an empty bay and checks crane reach before a live lift.
Safety concern drives **unease**; his own higher wage and strong reserve remain secure in steady change.

steps.text: Learn updated AI lift controls on unused site bay
Compare crane reach with tape measurements before overhead work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can plan the canopy, and capable robots around 2031 might fit it overhead. Contractors should publish the paid crew rota and safety rules before anyone is sent home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 63 when robots can do the physical work, four years before I hope to leave regular sites at 67 if our figures allow. Nine months saved and plenty of builders give us time, but a lost overhead premium could still shorten the income we planned on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the contractor for written canopy staffing and a protected robot trial area with a named worker able to halt lifts. If it offers a funded, recognised equipment-safety course with a real place and full wages through class days, I'll enrol; if my shifts are cut first, I'll apply only to posted local building jobs with safe duties and pay covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage cut before 67, with enough money to choose rather than grab the first offer. I would rather learn a tool properly than watch a sales clip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner what our reserve can do. Our nine-month reserve buys time after a canopy shift cut, not four years of wages. We would compare our retirement statements with actual bills before changing an exit date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which safeguards should a canopy robot trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trial would need a clear area below the canopy, a checked sling and a worker who can stop the robot. No one should walk under it until the timber has been fixed and tested.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans canopies before robots fit them around 2031.
Contractors should publish **paid crew rotas** and safe robot trial rules.
think: At about **63**, losing overhead premium could disturb our plan to work until around 67.
Nine months of **savings** and nearby builders help, but cannot replace years of wages.
do: **Ask** contractor for written canopy rota and protected stop-enabled robot trial.
**Enrol** in funded recognised equipment course if real place and full class wages secured.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local building job with safe duties and bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible income loss before retirement.
S2.quote: Our nine-month reserve buys time after a canopy shift cut, not four years of wages.
fieldNote: He faces a **credible wage risk** at about 63 despite high pay, savings and abundant nearby builders.
Training requires **funded fees**, a place and full wages; job applications follow cuts and need posted local safe work with adequate pay.

steps.text: Ask contractor for written canopy rota and protected stop-enabled robot trial
Enrol in funded recognised equipment course if real place and full class wages secured
Apply after cuts to posted local building job with safe duties and bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 may write the lift plan, and robots around 2034 might fit the canopy. Five years gives us time to test a robot on an actual beam and train the next crew safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 66 when robots can do the fitting, a year before I hope to stop if our household income holds. We have nine months saved, but I would still want a wage if retirement costs are higher than the statements suggest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll take a free evening introduction to site-machine controls this winter while keeping my canopy job. If the contractor funds a recognised inspection certificate with paid assessment days and an actual place, I'll enrol next year; after qualifying, if my shifts are cut and our retirement income is short, I'll apply only to posted local equipment-checking roles with safe hours and pay covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible final working-year gap, but willing to use the runway. The free class lets me learn without giving up a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the first machine lesson include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise the stop control on a grounded test beam with the trainer beside me. A robot lesson that never lets a carpenter touch the stop switch is no lesson at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an equipment job workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The local posting would need the actual weekly hours, safe lifting duties and a wage that covers our bills. If no such job is open, I'll keep the current canopy pay while it is offered.

say: **2031 thinking AI** writes lift plans before robots fit canopies around 2034.
Five years allows **hands-on stop training** on a grounded beam.
think: At about **66**, I might need one more year of wages.
Nine months of **savings** cannot settle every retirement-cost uncertainty.
do: **Attend** free evening site-machine controls class while employed.
**Enrol** in recognised inspection certificate if funded place and paid assessment days secured.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts if income short to posted local job with safe bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible last-year wage loss, with a training route.
S3.quote: A robot lesson that never lets a carpenter touch the stop switch is no lesson at all.
fieldNote: He begins **actual free study** now, then requires funded certification, paid assessment days and a real place for further training.
His job application requires **qualification and cuts** plus income shortfall plus a posted local vacancy with safe duties and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Enrol in recognised inspection certificate if funded place and paid assessment days secured
Apply after qualification and cuts if income short to posted local job with safe bill-covering pay
Check posted weekly hours, safe lifting duties and wages against household bills
Keep current paid canopy work while offered if no suitable posted role opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may plan canopies and capable robots around 2039 may fit them. I hope to be off regular sites by 67 if our money allows, so apprentices need a safe lift lesson before the older fitters leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 71 when robots could do the overhead work, beyond my hoped-for site years. Our current statements and nine-month reserve make leaving at 67 look plausible, though my partner and I will keep checking actual income and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my height-safety ticket current and finish the present site work while employed. At a local trade guild apprenticeship meeting I'll propose a paid ground-level canopy lift lesson; if our figures permit stopping at 67, I'll hand the support drawings to a younger fitter before my last site day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our present income and a robot date beyond the hoped-for exit. I can help the next carpenter learn without pretending I will be lifting canopies in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprentice practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have an apprentice check the sling and support on a grounded beam before any crane moves. A canopy robot can follow a perfect drawing and still leave a worker under a bad lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the guild lesson safe and paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guild lesson needs paid apprentice hours, a trainer and a clear area around a ground-level test beam. I would bring our current lift checklist to the meeting so the request is specific.

say: **2036 thinking AI** plans canopies before robots fit them around 2039.
A **paid ground-level lesson** would prepare younger carpenters safely.
think: At about **71**, robots likely arrive after my hoped-for exit at 67.
Current **retirement statements** look workable but still need checking against bills.
do: **Keep** height-safety ticket current while on present site rota.
**Propose** paid supervised canopy lesson at trade guild apprenticeship meeting.
**Hand** support drawings to younger fitter before exit if finances permit.
feel: **Calm** about present income, focused on a safe handover.
S4.quote: A canopy robot can follow a perfect drawing and still leave a worker under a bad lift.
fieldNote: His group lesson requires **paid apprentice hours** with a trainer and ground-level exclusion area, making safety and funding explicit.
He separates **current site work** and a conditional pre-exit handover from the robot date at about 71.

steps.text: Keep height-safety ticket current while on present site rota
Propose paid supervised canopy lesson at trade guild apprenticeship meeting
Hand support drawings to younger fitter before exit if finances permit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could take overhead shifts at about 63, before I hope to leave site work. A protected paid trial, funded safety training and posted local roles with safe duties and adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who stops a robot lift if the beam swings toward the walkway. A perfect lift plan is no shelter for the person standing below a loose sling. I want the stop control in a carpenter's hand.

headlineQuote: A perfect lift plan is no shelter for the person standing below a loose sling.
portrait: **Wei**, 58, is an experienced site carpenter fitting overhead canopies with a vocational certificate and higher shift pay.
His medical-practice partner and grown children share a **nine-month reserve**, with plentiful local builders nearby.
He uses **AI daily** for board lists and learns new lift controls early, while favouring paid craft apprenticeships.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about losing premiums before a conditional exit around 67; long timelines allow a safe handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring canopy robots around 2031 while he is about 63 and still needs overhead pay.
whatWouldHelp: A **protected paid trial**, funded safety training and posted local roles with safe duties and sufficient wages would help.
